To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GABAA and not GABAB receptors are critically involved in the generation of SWDs in the thalamus of the WAG/R ij rats, an animal model of absence epilepsy.
the two sub-types of GABAA receptors play a differential and opposite role during the two types of spike-wave paroxisms observed during absence seizures.
the GABAA receptors, but not the GABAB receptors in thalamocorticortical neurons of WAG/Rij rats, are responsible for the generation of spike and wave discharches during spontaneous absences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the contribution of GABA receptors in the thalamus to the pathophysiology of absence epilepsy.
the contribution of GABAA- and GABAB-receptor-mediated events to spike-and-wave discharges (SWD) during spontaneous absence seizures in the WAG/ Rij strain of rats.
the role of GABA receptors in the pathophysiology of generalized absence seizures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GABAA and the GABAB receptors play different roles in the generation and maintenance of SWD activity in the thalamic ventrobasal complex.
the GABAergic mechanisms involved in absence seizures are complex and may vary depending on the type of absence seizures, the brain region under investigation, and/or the animal model.
both subtypes of GABAA receptors are critically involved in the generation of SWDs in WAG/Rij rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the GABAA and the GABAB receptors have a different role in the generation of SWDs.
the thalamic GABAB receptor is involved in the generation of the slow spike and wave paroxysms, whereas the fast spike and wave discharging activity is mediated through GABAA receptors.

GABAB receptors are not critical for the generation of SWDs in thalamocortex, but that they may be critical in other brain regions, such as the reticular thalamic nucleus, which is not studied in this paper.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GABAergic mechanisms play a differential role during different types of absence seizures, with a critical contribution of GABAA receptors during fast spike-wave discharges.

, although the GABAB-mediated component of GABAergic transmission is important for the maintenance of the 3-Hz SWD in absence epilepsy, it is not essential for the generation of the 5–9-Hz SWD, which is the main hallmark of this pathology.
, in thalamic neurons, GABAA and, to a lesser extent, GABAB receptor activation are both involved in the generation of SWDs during spontaneous absence seizures.
